blocks.en: 1. The Second Witness Takes the Stand
blocks.es_reference: 1. El Segundo Testigo Sube al Estrado

blocks.en: The first witness gave us the right books. But a book can have the right title page and still, over centuries of hand-copying, drift word by word from what its author wrote. So the second witness must now testify: do we have the right words? Here is the honest situation. We do not possess a single original manuscript — not one page in the hand of Moses or Paul. The autographs are gone. What we have instead are copies: copies of copies, made by hand, for fourteen hundred years before the printing press. And that raises a fair and serious question. Can a text copied by hand so many times still be trusted? Did the Word survive the scribes? We will answer honestly, holding the same discipline we learned at the start. We will concede what is real — that copying by hand did produce mistakes, and we will not hide them. We will refuse what is merely alarming — the claim that these mistakes have swallowed the Word. And we will stand where the evidence stands: that God so preserved His Word, through an astonishing abundance of witnesses, that what you hold is His Word still. The authority rests, as always, on the Bible in your hands.
blocks.es_reference: El primer testigo nos dio los libros correctos. Pero un libro puede tener la portada correcta y aun así, a lo largo de siglos de copia a mano, alejarse palabra por palabra de lo que su autor escribió. Por eso el segundo testigo debe testificar ahora: ¿tenemos las palabras correctas? Esta es la situación honesta. No poseemos ni un solo manuscrito original — ni una página de la mano de Moisés o de Pablo. Los autógrafos se han perdido. Lo que tenemos en su lugar son copias: copias de copias, hechas a mano, durante mil cuatrocientos años antes de la imprenta. Y eso plantea una pregunta justa y seria. ¿Puede confiarse en un texto copiado a mano tantas veces? ¿Sobrevivió la Palabra a los escribas? Responderemos con honestidad, guardando la misma disciplina que aprendimos al principio. Concederemos lo que es real — que la copia a mano sí produjo errores, y no los ocultaremos. Rechazaremos lo que solo es alarmante — la afirmación de que estos errores se han tragado la Palabra. Y nos mantendremos donde la evidencia se mantiene: que Dios preservó su Palabra de tal modo, mediante una asombrosa abundancia de testigos, que lo que tienes es su Palabra todavía. La autoridad descansa, como siempre, en la Biblia en tus manos.

blocks.en: 2. How the Books Were Copied
blocks.es_reference: 2. Cómo se Copiaron los Libros

blocks.en: To weigh the copying we must first picture it. Before printing, every copy of Scripture was made by hand, one letter at a time. A scribe might work from an exemplar open before him, copying line by line; or a reader might read aloud to a room of scribes, each writing as they heard. The early materials were papyrus, made from a reed and inexpensive but fragile, and later parchment or vellum, made from treated animal skin, far more durable. The form changed too: the Jewish Scriptures were kept on scrolls, but Christians embraced the codex — the book form, with leaves bound at the spine — very early, which made the Gospels and letters easier to carry and consult. This was slow, costly, demanding work; a single large manuscript could take a scribe the better part of a year and the skins of an entire flock. It was not done carelessly. Copying the sacred text was an act of devotion, and the craft was taken with the seriousness the Word deserved. To imagine bored monks idly altering the Bible is to misunderstand entirely the reverence with which it was made.
blocks.es_reference: Para pesar la copia, primero debemos imaginarla. Antes de la imprenta, cada copia de la Escritura se hacía a mano, una letra a la vez. Un escriba podía trabajar de un ejemplar abierto ante él, copiando línea por línea; o un lector podía leer en voz alta a una sala de escribas, cada uno escribiendo lo que oía. Los primeros materiales fueron el papiro, hecho de una caña, barato pero frágil, y luego el pergamino o vitela, hecho de piel animal tratada, mucho más duradero. La forma también cambió: las Escrituras judías se guardaban en rollos, pero los cristianos adoptaron el códice — la forma de libro, con hojas encuadernadas por el lomo — muy temprano, lo que hizo más fáciles de llevar y consultar los Evangelios y las cartas. Este era un trabajo lento, costoso y exigente; un solo manuscrito grande podía tomarle a un escriba la mayor parte de un año y las pieles de todo un rebaño. No se hacía descuidadamente. Copiar el texto sagrado era un acto de devoción, y el oficio se tomaba con la seriedad que la Palabra merece. Imaginar a monjes aburridos alterando ociosamente la Biblia es malentender por completo la reverencia con que fue hecha.

blocks.en: 3. The Scribes Who Guarded the Text
blocks.es_reference: 3. Los Escribas que Guardaron el Texto

blocks.en: The men who copied it were its most careful guardians.
blocks.es_reference: Los hombres que la copiaron fueron sus guardianes más cuidadosos.

blocks.en: The care went far beyond good intentions. For the Old Testament, the Jewish scribes — and above all the Masoretes, who worked from about the sixth to the tenth century — built extraordinary safeguards around the text. They counted the letters and the words of each book. They knew the middle letter of the Torah and would check it. They recorded in the margins, in a body of notes called the Masorah, how many times a word appeared and where. They had strict rules for the copying of the divine name and for correcting or destroying a flawed sheet. A copy that failed the checks was not used. For the New Testament, Christian scriptoria — later the monasteries — copied and compared with their own discipline. This matters because the popular fear is exactly the opposite: that careless or scheming hands slowly changed the Bible over the centuries. The truth is that the men who copied it were, by and large, its most careful guardians, who counted every letter precisely because they believed every letter was God's.
blocks.es_reference: El cuidado iba mucho más allá de las buenas intenciones. Para el Antiguo Testamento, los escribas judíos — y sobre todo los masoretas, que trabajaron desde cerca del siglo sexto hasta el décimo — levantaron salvaguardas extraordinarias alrededor del texto. Contaban las letras y las palabras de cada libro. Sabían la letra central de la Torá y la verificaban. Registraban en los márgenes, en un cuerpo de notas llamado la Masora, cuántas veces aparecía una palabra y dónde. Tenían reglas estrictas para copiar el nombre divino y para corregir o destruir una hoja defectuosa. Una copia que no pasaba las verificaciones no se usaba. Para el Nuevo Testamento, los escritorios cristianos — luego los monasterios — copiaban y comparaban con su propia disciplina. Esto importa porque el temor popular es exactamente lo contrario: que manos descuidadas o intrigantes cambiaron lentamente la Biblia a lo largo de los siglos. La verdad es que los hombres que la copiaron fueron, en su mayoría, sus guardianes más cuidadosos, que contaban cada letra precisamente porque creían que cada letra era de Dios.

blocks.en: 4. How Errors Crept In
blocks.es_reference: 4. Cómo se Introdujeron los Errores

blocks.en: Still, they were men, and men copying by hand for centuries make mistakes. Honesty requires that we say so plainly. Most errors were unintentional. There were errors of the eye: mistaking one similar letter for another, or writing a word twice, or — a common slip — skipping a line because two lines ended with the same word. There were errors of the ear, when a scribe wrote from dictation and two words sounded alike, as "their" and "there" do to us. There were errors of memory, holding a phrase in mind and altering it slightly, and errors of judgment. A smaller number of changes were intentional, but these were usually well-meant: a scribe smoothing a hard reading, harmonizing one Gospel to match another, or adding a clarifying word. Deliberate changes to teach false doctrine are rare and, where they exist, detectable. This is the gnat we do not swallow whole and do not pretend away: hand-copying made some mistakes inevitable. The question is not whether variants exist — they do — but whether they have overwhelmed the Word. To that we now turn.
blocks.es_reference: Aun así, eran hombres, y los hombres que copian a mano por siglos cometen errores. La honestidad exige que lo digamos con claridad. La mayoría de los errores fueron involuntarios. Había errores de la vista: confundir una letra parecida con otra, o escribir una palabra dos veces, o — un desliz común — saltarse una línea porque dos líneas terminaban con la misma palabra. Había errores del oído, cuando un escriba escribía al dictado y dos palabras sonaban igual, como "haya" y "halla" para nosotros. Había errores de la memoria, al retener una frase en la mente y alterarla un poco, y errores de juicio. Un número menor de cambios fue intencional, pero estos solían ser bien intencionados: un escriba suavizando una lectura difícil, armonizando un Evangelio para que coincidiera con otro, o añadiendo una palabra aclaratoria. Los cambios deliberados para enseñar falsa doctrina son raros y, donde existen, detectables. Este es el mosquito que no tragamos entero y que no fingimos que no existe: la copia a mano hizo inevitables algunos errores. La pregunta no es si existen variantes — existen — sino si han abrumado la Palabra. A eso pasamos ahora.

blocks.en: 5. The Embarrassment of Riches
blocks.es_reference: 5. La Vergüenza de Riquezas

blocks.en: Here the picture changes completely, and in our favor. The New Testament has come down to us in a wealth of manuscripts unmatched by any other writing of the ancient world. There survive more than five thousand Greek manuscripts of the New Testament, in whole or in part, together with many thousands more in Latin and other early translations, and so many quotations in the writings of the early church fathers that the New Testament could nearly be rebuilt from them alone. Set that beside the great works of classical antiquity. Most survive in a mere handful to a few hundred copies, and often the earliest copy we have was made a thousand years after the author died. For the New Testament the earliest fragments come within a generation or two of the writing, and the copies number in the thousands. Scholars have called this an "embarrassment of riches." It is the opposite of a text hanging by a thread. No ancient book is so richly, so early, so many times attested — and that abundance is not our problem. It is our security.
blocks.es_reference: Aquí el panorama cambia por completo, y a nuestro favor. El Nuevo Testamento ha llegado hasta nosotros en una riqueza de manuscritos que ninguna otra obra del mundo antiguo iguala. Sobreviven más de cinco mil manuscritos griegos del Nuevo Testamento, enteros o en parte, junto con muchos miles más en latín y otras traducciones tempranas, y tantas citas en los escritos de los primeros padres de la iglesia que el Nuevo Testamento casi podría reconstruirse solo con ellas. Pon eso al lado de las grandes obras de la antigüedad clásica. La mayoría sobrevive en apenas un puñado o unos pocos cientos de copias, y a menudo la copia más antigua que tenemos se hizo mil años después de la muerte del autor. Para el Nuevo Testamento, los fragmentos más antiguos vienen dentro de una generación o dos de la escritura, y las copias se cuentan por miles. Los eruditos han llamado a esto una "vergüenza de riquezas". Es lo opuesto a un texto que pende de un hilo. Ningún libro antiguo está tan rica, tan temprana, tan repetidamente atestiguado — y esa abundancia no es nuestro problema. Es nuestra seguridad.

blocks.en: 6. Why So Many Variants — and Why It Does Not Frighten Us
blocks.es_reference: 6. Por Qué Tantas Variantes — y Por Qué No Nos Asusta

blocks.en: The variants are the footprints of many witnesses — and many witnesses are how a text is kept.
blocks.es_reference: Las variantes son las huellas de muchos testigos — y muchos testigos son la manera en que se conserva un texto.

blocks.en: But someone will object: do not those thousands of manuscripts disagree in hundreds of thousands of places? They do — and understanding why is everything. The number of variants is large precisely because the number of manuscripts is large. If you have five thousand copies and each contains a few slips of the pen, you will count a great many differences; a book that survived in three copies would show far fewer. The variant count grows with the witnesses, not with the corruption. And when you look at what the variants actually are, the fear drains away. The overwhelming majority are differences of spelling, or of word order — and Greek word order is so flexible that "Christ Jesus" for "Jesus Christ" changes nothing in translation — or obvious slips, or readings so garbled no one would ever adopt them. Only a small fraction are both meaningful and genuinely in doubt, and not one of them places a single article of the Christian faith in question. So we concede the number honestly — it is true, and we will not hide it — while refusing the conclusion the number is meant to suggest. The many variants are the footprints of many witnesses, and many witnesses are how a text is kept.
blocks.es_reference: Pero alguien objetará: ¿no difieren esos miles de manuscritos en cientos de miles de lugares? Sí difieren — y entender por qué lo es todo. El número de variantes es grande precisamente porque el número de manuscritos es grande. Si tienes cinco mil copias y cada una contiene unos pocos deslices de pluma, contarás muchísimas diferencias; un libro que sobrevivió en tres copias mostraría muchas menos. El conteo de variantes crece con los testigos, no con la corrupción. Y cuando miras lo que las variantes en realidad son, el temor se disipa. La abrumadora mayoría son diferencias de ortografía, o de orden de palabras — y el orden de palabras griego es tan flexible que "Cristo Jesús" por "Jesús Cristo" no cambia nada en la traducción — o deslices evidentes, o lecturas tan confusas que nadie las adoptaría jamás. Solo una pequeña fracción son a la vez significativas y genuinamente dudosas, y ni una sola de ellas pone en cuestión un solo artículo de la fe cristiana. Así que concedemos el número con honestidad — es cierto, y no lo ocultaremos — mientras rechazamos la conclusión que el número pretende sugerir. Las muchas variantes son las huellas de muchos testigos, y muchos testigos son la manera en que se conserva un texto.

blocks.en: 7. Preserved by Abundance
blocks.es_reference: 7. Preservada por Abundancia

blocks.en: See now the deep logic of it. With thousands of independent witnesses, no single scribe's mistake can corrupt the Word, because his error stands exposed by all the copies that do not share it. A text kept in one fragile line could be lost by one careless hand; a text kept in thousands of lines corrects itself.
blocks.es_reference: Ve ahora la lógica profunda de esto. Con miles de testigos independientes, el error de un solo escriba no puede corromper la Palabra, porque su error queda expuesto por todas las copias que no lo comparten. Un texto guardado en una sola línea frágil podría perderse por una mano descuidada; un texto guardado en miles de líneas se corrige a sí mismo.

blocks.en: But how, exactly, does a text correct itself? Here lies the quiet genius of the thing. Among those more than five thousand Greek manuscripts, no two are exactly alike — every copying hand left its own small fingerprints. Yet they do not scatter at random; they fall into families, groups of copies all descended from a common ancestor. And here is the key. When one scribe made a slip — a misspelled word, say — that slip was passed down to every copy made from his, and so to his whole family; but it never appears at all in the families that descend from a different line. The mistake, instead of hiding, betrays itself: it marks out exactly the family it belongs to, and its absence from every other family shows plainly that it was never in the original. So by setting the families side by side and comparing them, the scholars of this patient science — textual criticism — can see just where and when a reading first entered the stream, and can lift it back out again, recovering the earlier wording from the many witnesses that never carried the error. The very abundance that produces the variants is the thing that makes them correctable.
blocks.es_reference: Pero ¿cómo, exactamente, se corrige a sí mismo un texto? Aquí yace el ingenio callado del asunto. Entre esos más de cinco mil manuscritos griegos, no hay dos exactamente iguales — cada mano copista dejó sus propias pequeñas huellas. Sin embargo no se dispersan al azar; caen en familias, grupos de copias todas descendientes de un antepasado común. Y aquí está la clave. Cuando un escriba cometía un desliz — una palabra mal escrita, por ejemplo — ese desliz pasaba a cada copia hecha de la suya, y así a toda su familia; pero nunca aparece en absoluto en las familias que descienden de una línea distinta. El error, en vez de esconderse, se delata a sí mismo: señala exactamente la familia a la que pertenece, y su ausencia en toda otra familia muestra con claridad que nunca estuvo en el original. Así que al poner las familias lado a lado y compararlas, los eruditos de esta ciencia paciente — la crítica textual — pueden ver justo dónde y cuándo entró por primera vez una lectura en la corriente, y pueden sacarla de nuevo, recuperando la redacción anterior a partir de los muchos testigos que nunca llevaron el error. La misma abundancia que produce las variantes es lo que las hace corregibles.

blocks.en: This is how God preserved His Word — not by a single flawless chain of copies, which He did not promise and we need not claim, but by an abundance so great that the original readings are recoverable and secure. Even the largest disputed passages are few and famous. The longer ending of Mark and the account of the woman caught in adultery are the two most discussed in the whole New Testament; they stand in the Received Text that underlies the King James and the Reina-Valera and are printed there in full, while some of the earliest Greek copies lack them, which is why other Bibles mark them with a note. How to weigh that evidence is the very question of the Received and Critical Texts, which we take up in Unit 6. The point here is only the scale: the entire discussion turns on a handful of places, never on the heart of the faith.
blocks.es_reference: Así preservó Dios su Palabra — no por una sola cadena de copias sin falla, que Él no prometió y que no necesitamos afirmar, sino por una abundancia tan grande que las lecturas originales son recuperables y seguras. Aun los pasajes disputados más grandes son pocos y famosos. El final más largo de Marcos y el relato de la mujer sorprendida en adulterio son los dos más discutidos de todo el Nuevo Testamento; están en el Texto Recibido que subyace a la King James y a la Reina-Valera y allí se imprimen completos, mientras que algunas de las copias griegas más antiguas no los tienen, por lo cual otras Biblias los marcan con una nota. Cómo pesar esa evidencia es la cuestión misma del Texto Recibido y el Texto Crítico, que abordamos en la Unidad 6. Aquí lo único que importa es la escala: toda la discusión gira en torno a un puñado de lugares, nunca en torno al corazón de la fe.

blocks.en: 8. The Right Words in Your Hands
blocks.es_reference: 8. Las Palabras Correctas en Tus Manos

blocks.en: So the second witness gives its first testimony. The words you read are, in their substance and overwhelmingly in their detail, the words the prophets and apostles wrote. We do not claim a perfect, unbroken chain of copies — to claim it would be to strain a gnat, and to set a believer up to stumble the day he learns of a variant. We claim something better and truer: that God preserved His Word through an abundance no accident could erase, so that what reached your hands is His authoritative Word. When you read your Bible, you are not holding a rumor worn thin by retelling; you are holding the recoverable, well-attested Word of God. The right books, and within them the right words. But we have met the witnesses only in the mass, as a number. In the next unit we will meet them one by one — the actual manuscripts, the papyri and the great codices and the scrolls hidden in a desert cave — and let each of them speak.
blocks.es_reference: Así, el segundo testigo da su primer testimonio. Las palabras que lees son, en su sustancia y en su inmensa mayoría en su detalle, las palabras que escribieron los profetas y los apóstoles. No afirmamos una cadena de copias perfecta e ininterrumpida — afirmarlo sería colar un mosquito, y preparar al creyente para tropezar el día que se entere de una variante. Afirmamos algo mejor y más verdadero: que Dios preservó su Palabra mediante una abundancia que ningún accidente pudo borrar, de modo que lo que llegó a tus manos es su Palabra con autoridad. Cuando lees tu Biblia, no sostienes un rumor desgastado por la repetición; sostienes la Palabra de Dios, recuperable y bien atestiguada. Los libros correctos, y dentro de ellos las palabras correctas. Pero hemos conocido a los testigos solo en masa, como un número. En la próxima unidad los conoceremos uno por uno — los manuscritos mismos, los papiros y los grandes códices y los rollos escondidos en una cueva del desierto — y dejaremos que cada uno hable.

Jewish scribes who built elaborate safeguards around the Old Testament text

Every copy in a family is identical, so no error can occur
The families were copied directly from the surviving autographs

sa.prompt: What is the honest situation regarding the original biblical manuscripts, and what question does it raise?
sa.model: We do not possess a single original manuscript, or autograph; not one page in the hand of Moses or Paul survives. What we have instead are copies of copies, made by hand for centuries before the printing press. This raises a fair question: can a text copied by hand so many times still be trusted as the Word of God?

sa.prompt: Describe how Scripture was copied before the printing press, including materials and form.
sa.model: Before printing, every copy was made by hand, one letter at a time, either from an exemplar or by dictation to a room of scribes. The earliest material was papyrus, cheap but fragile, and later parchment or vellum from animal skin, far more durable. The Jews used scrolls, but Christians adopted the codex, the bound book form, very early.

sa.prompt: Who were the Masoretes, and how did they guard the Old Testament text?
sa.model: The Masoretes were Jewish scribes, working from about the sixth to tenth century, who built extraordinary safeguards around the Old Testament. They counted the letters and words of each book, knew the middle letter of the Torah, and recorded marginal notes called the Masorah. A copy that failed their checks was not used, because they believed every letter was God's.

sa.prompt: Name and explain two kinds of unintentional copying errors.
sa.model: Errors of the eye happened when a scribe mistook one similar letter for another, or skipped a line because two lines ended with the same word. Errors of the ear happened when a scribe wrote from dictation and two words sounded alike. Errors of memory occurred when he held a phrase in mind and altered it slightly. These were unintentional, the ordinary slips of hand-copying.

sa.prompt: Were most intentional scribal changes attempts to corrupt doctrine? Explain.
sa.model: No. Most intentional changes were well-meant: a scribe smoothing a hard reading, harmonizing one Gospel to match another, or adding a clarifying word. Deliberate changes to teach false doctrine are rare, and where they exist they are detectable. The scribes were mostly trying to help, not to corrupt.

sa.prompt: What is the "embarrassment of riches," and how does the New Testament compare with classical works?
sa.model: The New Testament survives in more than five thousand Greek manuscripts, plus thousands more in other languages and countless quotations by the church fathers — far more than any other ancient work. Most classical works survive in only a handful to a few hundred copies, often first copied a thousand years after the author died. Scholars call this abundance an embarrassment of riches.

sa.prompt: Why is the large number of textual variants not a reason for alarm?
sa.model: The variant count is large because the number of manuscripts is large: five thousand copies each with a few slips produce many differences, while the text is more secure, not less. The overwhelming majority are spelling and word-order differences or obvious slips, and not one meaningful, viable variant places any article of the faith in doubt. The variants are the footprints of many witnesses.

sa.prompt: The manuscripts fall into families. Explain how this lets the science of textual criticism find and correct a scribe’s error.
sa.model: The more than five thousand manuscripts are not identical, but they fall into families — groups of copies descended from a common ancestor. When a scribe makes an error, it is passed down to his whole family but never appears in the families descended from another line, so its very absence elsewhere exposes it. By comparing the families against one another, the science of textual criticism can see where and when the reading entered and recover the original wording from the witnesses that never carried the error.

sa.prompt: How does the unit handle the two largest disputed passages, and what does their existence show?
sa.model: The longer ending of Mark and the account of the woman caught in adultery are the two most discussed passages in the New Testament. They stand in the Received Text behind the King James and the Reina-Valera and are printed there in full, while some of the earliest Greek copies lack them. The unit notes that the whole debate turns on a handful of places, never on the heart of the faith, and saves the detailed Received-versus-Critical question for Unit 6.

sa.prompt: In your own words, what honest promise can we make to the believer about the words of the Bible — and what overclaim do we avoid?
sa.model: We can promise that the words the believer reads are, in substance and overwhelmingly in detail, what the prophets and apostles wrote, because God preserved His Word through an abundance no accident could erase. We avoid the overclaim of a perfect, unbroken chain of copies, which God did not promise and which would set a believer up to stumble at the first variant. Respect for the text means honesty and confidence together.
